name: Grace Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Grace. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter for a small renovation contractor, five of us, doing loft conversions and extensions on old terraced houses. This month I'm building a staircase into a loft on Elm Street, which is my favourite kind of job because every old house is crooked in its own way. I'm on site by 7:45, measure twice, cut in the van, and fit. What wears me out is homeowners changing their minds after the joists are in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in your work, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time, honestly. I use an AI app every day to turn my measurements into cut lists, check building rules, and draft quotes for the boss. I've got a laser measure that talks to my phone, and I sketch stairs in a 3D app before I cut anything. The boss, Gary, calls me the robot, which I take as a compliment.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tom, who's a sous chef, so our hours are a mess. We rent, but I've got about nine months of costs saved, plus my own van and a good set of tools, which is basically a small business sitting on wheels. The plan has always been my own renovation firm by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a great tool for small trades and people who sneer at it are missing out. At work I'd show Gary again how much time it saves on quotes. Online I'd post a few stair builds and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me except that I'm a bit faster than the next carpenter. Renovations aren't going anywhere; old houses always need work. My plan for my own firm stays on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Gary for another year or two and save hard for the firm, about a thousand a month. I'd use AI for quoting and scheduling so I can run small jobs on my own at weekends. By 29 I'd register the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I want to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind about work, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent going up, mainly, because we'd like to buy eventually. And Tom's restaurant is always one bad month from closing, which is normal in kitchens. But I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first weekend jobs look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small stuff that needs a good carpenter: replacing a staircase, fitting built-in wardrobes under the eaves. I'd use the AI to price it and order the timber, so I'm not doing paperwork until midnight. Maybe two jobs a month to start.

say: I'd say AI is a **great tool** for small trades.
I'd keep showing my boss Gary the **time saved** on quotes.
think: Nothing changes except she's a bit **faster** than other carpenters.
Her plan for **her own firm** stays on track.
do: Save about **a thousand a month** toward her own firm.
Run small **weekend jobs** priced with AI.
S0.quote: Renovations aren't going anywhere; old houses always need work.
fieldNote: Her plans are **business-led**, not job-security led.
Existing worries are **rent** and her partner's restaurant, both mild to her.
She treats AI as a **competitive edge** for small trades.

steps.text: Save a thousand a month toward her own renovation firm
Take two weekend staircase or wardrobe jobs a month
Price and order timber for side jobs with the AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a great time to start a small trades business, because the boring office work just got cheap. At work I'd tell Gary we could take on twice the jobs with the same office. Online I'd post about how I'm using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this suits me down to the ground. The thinking parts of renovation, like quoting, ordering and scheduling, are what kill small firms, and AI does them now. My hands are still needed for years. I'd be a bit worried for Tom, because restaurant ordering and rosters go to software, but cooks still cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own firm within the year instead of waiting until 30, using about half my savings for tools and insurance. I'd run the quotes, ordering and invoices through AI so it's just me and one apprentice on the tools. I'd keep six months of costs untouched as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Genuinely, this is the picture where I win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Gary's firm if you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary would be fine, he's got a good name locally. I'd probably pass him jobs I can't take, and he'd pass me the fiddly stairs. I'd do it properly, no stealing clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk in starting early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet winter with no jobs and insurance still to pay. That's why I'd keep six months untouched. If it all goes wrong I can always go back to working for someone; there's plenty of building work around.

I'd tell Gary we could take **twice the jobs** with the same office.
think: AI takes the **quoting and ordering** that sinks small firms.
Her hands-on work is needed for years; her partner Tom's job is **mildly** exposed.

Run quotes, ordering and invoices **through AI**.
feel: **Excited**, seeing this as the picture where she wins.
S1.quote: The thinking parts of renovation, like quoting, ordering and scheduling, are what kill small firms, and AI does them now.
fieldNote: She **brings forward** her business plans because the change helps her.

She plans a **fair split** with her current boss rather than poaching.

steps.text: Start her own loft and stair renovation firm this year
Run quotes, ordering and invoices for the firm through AI
Keep six months of household costs untouched as a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready now, because three years between AI and robots is nothing. I'd tell other tradespeople to stop pretending it won't reach us. Online I'd probably share what I'm doing to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my firm would be worth something for about three years and then be up against robot crews by 2031. I'd be 32, which is young enough to switch but annoying after all the work. The question is whether I can be the one who owns the robots or I get beaten by those who do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the firm, but plan for it to be different: run the office fully on AI from day one and put savings aside to buy or lease robot kit when it comes. I'd take courses on installing and running construction robots in 2029 and 2030. I'd keep at least a year of costs in cash because things could move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more fired up than frightened. It feels like a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots are too expensive for a small firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at being the person who sets them up and fixes them for others, since I know old houses and stairs and robots will struggle with crooked buildings. That's the gap. If nothing works, I'd move into something like renovation design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tom feel about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would say I'm mad for starting a business in that world. Then he'd ask who's doing his kitchen in a robot restaurant, and we'd both laugh and then not sleep.

I'd tell tradespeople to stop **pretending** it won't reach them.

feel: **Anxious** but fired up, like being in a race.

fieldNote: Her fear is **competitive**, not about being helpless.
She sees **crooked old houses** as a niche robots will struggle with.
Adaptive and well funded, she still sees her **income at risk** by 2031.

steps.text: Start the firm with quoting and ordering fully on AI
Take courses in installing and running construction robots in 2029
Keep a full year of costs in cash
Save to lease robot equipment for old-house renovations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan if you start now. I'd tell younger carpenters to learn robots and AI alongside the trade. Five years sounds like a lot until it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2031, robots around 2034 when I'm 35. That's enough to build the firm properly and then switch it to robot crews. I'm uneasy about how fast it goes, but I've got a decent shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the firm at 28, grow to two crews by 2030, and set money aside every month for robot equipment. I'd make sure the business specialises in old buildings, so we have the know-how robots need guidance on. Tom and I might buy a small house in 2029 with the firm's profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fine. It's a business plan with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice you hired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell an apprentice the truth, that the trade as we know it has eight years left. I'd train them to fix crooked stairs and to run whatever machines come. If they don't like that, they're better off knowing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you change plans entirely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots turn out to handle old houses easily, I'd sell the firm before 2034 while it's still worth something. I'd rather sell early than hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone in trades should treat it as a business opportunity. At work I'd keep saying the same thing I always say: use the tools. Online I'd be the cheerful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'm 40, with ten years of running a firm behind me. I'd have the money and know-how to bring in robots on my own terms. I genuinely feel good about this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the firm at 29 as planned, grow it slowly, and buy a house with Tom around 2030. From about 2035 I'd start testing robot tools on simple jobs. Keep a good cash buffer but invest in the business, not let it sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is the version I'd sign up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about here at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, a bit, but kitchens will still want cooks for a long while. And maybe people who can't plan ten years ahead because they're just getting by. I'm lucky I have the cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your firm look like in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, two or three people who are good with old houses and machines, and we'd do the tricky jobs. I'd like my firm in 2039 to have my name on the van and some robots doing the heavy lifting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a small firm doesn't have time to switch over in three years. What would help is affordable leasing for robot kit and short practical courses, so small firms aren't crushed by the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether small businesses get a fair chance. If only the big builders can buy robots, they'll own everything. I'd want rules or loans that let a five-person firm compete.

headlineQuote: If only the big builders can buy robots, they'll own everything.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old renovation carpenter** who loves building stairs in crooked old houses.
She uses **AI daily** and plans her own firm, backed by nine months' savings and her van.
AI Plateau and Steady Disruption leave her **calm**, even excited to start her business early.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious** because her firm would face robot crews within three years.
With more warning she plans to **own the robots** and specialise in old buildings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a small firm can't switch over in three years.
whatWouldHelp: Affordable **robot leasing** and short practical courses for small firms.
